name: Liam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the depot on the ring road by half six, loading a white van for Swiftline, which is a subcontractor that does the last bit for one of the big parcel networks. The scanner gives me about 140 stops, and the order it picks is the order I drive, even when it makes no sense. I've only been doing it eighteen months, so I'm still slower than the old hands, especially in the new estates where the house numbers jump around. I get back around six, eat whatever Noor, my girlfriend, left before her night shift at the care home, and fall asleep on the sofa.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The thing that wears me out is the scanner timing me. If I spend four minutes finding a flat with no number on the door, the little bar goes red and the supervisor gets a message. What I like is the bit nobody sees: the old man on Cedar Lane who waits at the window for his tablets, the dog that knows my van. I like being out, not stuck under a strip light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the last thing we need is another gadget squeezing us. At the depot, half the lads already think AI is just a new name for the scanner that times us. I'd probably post something like "told you it was hype" and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI being hype doesn't fix my problem, because my problem was never AI. My problem is Swiftline cutting the day rate and adding stops every spring, and that keeps happening with or without clever computers. My job's still there, but it gets a bit worse every year and I can't see it getting better on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the same route and keep paying into the savings pot Noor and I set up, which is about three months of rent and bills right now. I'd go to the next couriers' union meeting at the community centre, which I keep meaning to do and never do because I'm knackered. I'm not changing jobs over this. I don't really know how to do anything else yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, I suppose. Relieved that nothing big is coming, but tired, because the normal version is already hard enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the day rate gets cut every spring. What happened the last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March they dropped it by ten a day and called it a "route efficiency update". Nobody asked us. Two drivers left, and their stops got split between the rest of us, so I was out till eight for a fortnight. Even if AI turns out to be hype, Swiftline (the parcel firm he drives for) will still find a way to squeeze ten more stops out of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Sami, who's been driving for Swiftline six years and actually reads the union leaflets. He keeps saying if ten of us joined, they'd have to talk to us. I believe him, I just haven't signed the form, which I know is daft.

say: I'd tell the depot that AI being **hype** is good news for drivers.
I'd post that the real problem is **pay cuts**, not clever computers.
think: Privately, my job **survives**, but Swiftline keeps adding stops and cutting the **day rate** anyway.
I can't see things getting **better** on their own, AI or no AI.
do: Keep driving the **same route** and keep the three-month savings pot topped up.
Go to the **union meeting** at the community centre instead of skipping it.
feel: **Relieved** nothing big is coming, but **tired** because normal is already hard.
S0.quote: Even if AI turns out to be hype, Swiftline (the parcel firm he drives for) will still find a way to squeeze ten more stops out of my day.
fieldNote: His worries are about **pay cuts** and stop targets, which he sees as unrelated to AI.
He supports the **union** in principle but hasn't joined; he admits the gap himself.
His three months of **savings** give him breathing room, so he doesn't feel cornered yet.

steps.text: Keep driving the Swiftline parcel route on the same day rate
Keep topping up the shared savings pot with Noor each month
Sign the couriers' union form Sami keeps handing out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the people who own the apps getting richer while we get the scraps. I'd share the union's posts about it and say the government should make companies share the savings. At the depot I'd say, "They'll replace the office before they replace us."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office does go first, and that's not great for me either, because the office is who I ring when a parcel's damaged. If the routing and complaints are all software, nobody's left to fight my corner when the bar goes red. My driving stays, but the rules around it get colder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the union form properly this time, the first week. I'd stop eating takeaway on shift and bring sandwiches, which saves about forty a week. I'm not going on any AI course, because I wouldn't understand it and I don't want to. I'd keep driving and hope the robots really are slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise in the engine and you turn the radio up so you don't have to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd turn the radio up. What would make you actually look under the bonnet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put one of those little robot carts in our depot, I'd look. Sami says a firm across town is trying them on student streets already. Until I see one with my own eyes, I'm not changing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Noor think when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor thinks care work is safer than mine, and she's probably right, because a robot isn't going to wash her residents any time soon. She says I should do the care certificate like her. I said I'd rather drive, and she gave me that look.

say: I'd say the app owners **keep the savings** while drivers get the scraps.
I'd tell the depot that the **office** will be replaced before the drivers.
think: The **office** going first hurts me too, because nobody will be left to fight my corner.
My **driving** stays for now, but the rules around it get colder and stricter.
do: Sign the **union form** in the first week instead of putting it off.
Bring sandwiches instead of takeaway, saving about **forty a week**.
Skip any **AI course** and keep driving, hoping the robots stay slow.
feel: **Uneasy**, like ignoring a strange noise from the engine with the radio turned up.
S1.quote: If the routing and complaints are all software, nobody's left to fight my corner when the bar goes red.
fieldNote: He sees the loss of **office staff** as a loss of protection, not just their jobs.
He refuses training outright and admits he's **hoping** the robots stay slow.
His girlfriend's suggestion of **care work** is the only real alternative he mentions, and he resists it.

steps.text: Join the couriers' union in the first week
Pack sandwiches instead of buying takeaway on shift
Watch for robot carts at the depot before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government with a backbone. I'd be posting that the tech firms should pay for everyone they put out of work. I'd be loud about it, louder than I've ever been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as a driver by 2031, when I'm thirty-two, and I'd have nothing else on my CV. The thinking part of my job is tiny, the scanner already does it, so the first three years I'd still be driving while everything around me falls apart. Then the robots come for the bit I actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those first three years I'd save everything I could, maybe get us to six months, and stop the holiday Noor and I were planning. I'd go to every union meeting and every protest about a jobs guarantee. I'd probably do the care certificate after all, but only when I had no choice, because I hate learning new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. It's the first time I'd feel like the floor's actually moving and I can't do anything about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the care certificate only when you had no choice. When would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the day Swiftline sends the letter, which is too late, I know. Noor would want me to start in the first year. I'd drag my feet until something forced me, because that's how I've always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor the night the letter came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend I should have listened to her about the care certificate, and that we'll be fine on her wages for a bit. Then I'd lie awake doing the sums. Her care home pays less than Swiftline, so we'd be eating into the savings within a couple of months.

say: I'd say we need **unions** and a government with a backbone.
I'd post that **tech firms** should pay for every worker they replace.
think: Privately, I expect to be **finished** as a driver by **2031**, at thirty-two.
My job is mostly **hands-on**, so I get three years, but nothing else on my CV.
do: Save hard to reach **six months** of savings and cancel the planned holiday.
Go to every **union meeting** and protest for a jobs guarantee.
Do the **care certificate**, but only once Swiftline's letter forces it.
feel: **Scared**, because the floor is moving and he feels he can't stop it.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend I should have listened to her about the care certificate, and that we'll be fine on her wages for a bit.
fieldNote: He sees the three years of **robot lag** as a stay of execution, not a chance.
He knows he'll **delay retraining** until forced and says so plainly.
The household would lean on his girlfriend's **lower care wage**, which worries him most.

steps.text: Cancel the planned holiday and save toward six months of bills
Go to every couriers' union meeting at the community centre
Join protests calling for a government jobs guarantee
Start the care certificate once Swiftline sends the redundancy letter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: unions, regulation, make the firms pay. I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd share every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years doesn't change much for me, because I wouldn't use them well. I'd be thirty-five when the robots come for driving, which is worse in a way, because I'd be older starting over. The extra time helps people who plan, and I'm not a planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, and maybe aim for a year's savings by 2034. I'd join the union and stay in it. I might do one evening of the care course to see if I can stand it, but I'd probably stop after a few weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like knowing about a dentist appointment for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably quit the course. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be on the van all day and then sitting in a classroom at seven feeling stupid. I left school at sixteen and I still hate that feeling. Noor would push me and I'd make excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Sami or someone from the depot did it with me, I'd stick it. On my own, I'd find reasons. I'm better when I'm in a group.

say: I'd say five years is **no excuse** for the government not having a plan.
I'd keep sharing **petitions** for regulation and making firms pay.
think: The extra time **won't help** me much, because I'm not a planner.
I'd be **thirty-five** when robots take driving, older and starting over.
do: Keep driving and build savings toward **a year** of bills by 2034.
Try an **evening care course**, though he expects to quit within weeks.
feel: **Heavy**, like waiting five years for a dentist appointment he dreads.
S3.quote: The extra time helps people who plan, and I'm not a planner.
fieldNote: He sees the extra years as **wasted** on himself and says it before being asked.
He'd stick with retraining only if a **workmate** joined him, showing he leans on groups.
His mood doesn't ease much, because he still expects to **lose driving** at thirty-five.

steps.text: Build savings toward a full year of rent and bills by 2034
Stay a paying member of the couriers' union
Try an evening care course with Sami from the depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper warning and the government has to use it: training paid for by the firms, a guaranteed wage while you learn. I'd be pushing the union to bargain for that. Online I'd say this is the chance to do it fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, ten years feels like enough time to do the care thing properly, even for me. I'd be thirty-seven before robots drive the vans, and maybe Noor and I would have kids by then, which makes it scarier. But it doesn't feel like a cliff any more, more like a long hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for a few years and do the care certificate part-time in the second or third year, with Sami if he'd come. I'd keep saving, and we'd probably wait a bit longer on kids. I'd vote for whoever promised paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's a slower worry. I can breathe with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor wants kids by thirty, and I said let's see what work looks like first. If driving's ending, I'd want one of us steady before a baby. That's the bit that actually keeps me up, more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old man on Cedar Lane waiting for his tablets. A robot can drop a box, but it won't notice when the old man on Cedar Lane (a street on his route) hasn't opened his curtains. That's the bit of the job that's actually mine.

say: I'd say ten years is a **proper warning** the government must use.
I'd push the union for **paid retraining** funded by the firms.
think: Ten years feels like enough to do **care work** properly, even for me.
Robots arrive when I'm **thirty-seven**, possibly with kids, which feels scarier.
do: Do the **care certificate** part-time in the second or third year.
Keep saving and **wait longer** on having kids with Noor.
feel: Still **worried**, but a slower worry he can breathe with.
S4.quote: A robot can drop a box, but it won't notice when the old man on Cedar Lane (a street on his route) hasn't opened his curtains.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear from a **cliff** into a long hill, in his own words.
**Starting a family** with his girlfriend becomes the real stake, more than the job itself.
He values the **human contact** on his route and sees it as the part robots can't do.

steps.text: Do the care certificate part-time in year two or three
Keep adding to the savings pot every payday
Put off having kids until one of them has steady work
Vote for parties promising paid retraining for drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have three years and I know I'd waste the first two. What would help is someone telling me exactly which course, paying me while I do it, and putting me in a class with people from the depot. Nobody should leave a van driver to work out the next job alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Noor's job, and that matters. Everyone talks about drivers, but if care homes start using robots too, we're both gone. I'd want someone looking at couples like us, not just one job at a time.

headlineQuote: Nobody should leave a van driver to work out the next job alone.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** parcel van driver for a subcontractor, still slower than the experienced drivers.
He lives with **Noor**, a night-shift care worker, and they share about three months of savings.
He backs **unions** and regulation, yet hasn't signed the union form, a gap he admits.
He avoids **new technology** and expects to delay retraining until he's forced into it.
His fear rises from **uneasy** about pay cuts to alarmed in the fast AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have three years and expects to waste the first two.
whatWouldHelp: A named, **paid course**, taken with workmates from the depot, so he isn't left alone.
Planning that looks at **couples** like him and Noor, not just one job.
